title: The Rock Cycle
summary: How igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks form and slowly change from one type into another in the never-ending rock cycle.
poll: Rocks are one thing in nature that never really changes.

versions.title: Rocks Can Change
versions.text:
A rock looks like it will last for all time. But rocks change. It just takes a long, long time. A rock can turn from one kind to the next. It goes round and round. That is a cycle. We call it the rock cycle.

Deep in the Earth, it is very hot. Rock melts there. Hot, melted rock is magma. It can come out of the ground. Then it is lava. The lava cools. It gets hard. Now it is new rock. Near Madinah, you can see big fields of this black rock.

Wind and rain hit rock. Bit by bit, they break it. Small bits like sand and mud wash away. They sink in a lake or the sea. They make a layer. More layers form on top. The weight packs them down. In time, they turn to rock. This rock may hold a fossil, like a shell.

Deep down, rock can get squeezed. It can get very hot. It does not melt. But it turns into a new kind of rock.

If rock melts, it is magma once more. The cycle goes on and on. It has no start and no end.

versions.title: Rocks Can Change
versions.text:
A rock may look like it will last forever. But rocks do change. It just takes a very long time. Rocks change from one kind to another. They go around in a cycle. It is called the rock cycle.

Deep inside the Earth, it is very hot. Rock melts there. Hot, melted rock under the ground is called magma. When it comes out of a volcano, it is called lava. The lava cools and gets hard. Now it is new rock. Near Madinah, there are huge fields of black rock. They formed this way.

Wind, rain, and ice wear rock down all the time. Bit by bit, they break it. They make tiny bits, like sand and mud. Water carries the bits away. They sink to the bottom of a lake or the sea. There they pile up in a layer. Then more layers form on top. The weight packs them down, and they slowly turn into rock. This rock may hold a fossil, like a shell.

Deep down, rock can get squeezed and very hot. It does not melt. But it changes into a new kind of rock.

If any rock melts, it is magma again. So the cycle goes on and on. It has no start and no end.

versions.title: The Rock Cycle
versions.text:
A rock may look like it will stay the same forever. But rocks are always changing. The change is just very slow. It can take millions of years. Rocks change from one kind to another in a loop that never ends. This loop is called the rock cycle.

Deep inside the Earth, it is hot enough to melt rock. Melted rock under the ground is called magma. When it comes out of a volcano, it is called lava. The lava cools. It gets hard and turns into new rock. Near Madinah, there are huge fields of black rock that formed from old lava.

Wind, rain, and ice wear rocks down all the time. They break them into tiny bits such as sand and mud. Water and wind carry the bits away. In lakes and seas, the bits sink and pile up in a layer. More layers form on top. Over a long time, the weight presses the layers together. They turn into rock. This rock often holds a fossil, such as a shell.

Deep under the ground, rock can be squeezed and heated. It does not melt, but it changes into a new kind of rock.

If any rock melts, it becomes magma again. Then the cycle starts over. The rock cycle has no start and no end.

versions.title: The Rock Cycle
versions.text:
A mountain may look like it will stay the same forever. But the rocks in it are slowly changing. The changes are so slow that they can take millions of years. Rocks change from one kind to another in a never-ending loop called the rock cycle. There are three main kinds of rock.

The first kind forms from fire. Deep inside the Earth, it is hot enough to melt rock. Melted rock underground is called magma. When it bursts out of a volcano, it is called lava. As the lava cools, it hardens into new rock. Near Madinah, there are huge fields of black rock that formed from ancient lava.

The second kind forms from tiny pieces. Wind, rain, and ice wear rocks down. They break them into bits such as sand and mud. Water carries the pieces away to lakes and seas. There the bits sink and pile up in a layer. More layers form on top. Over time, the weight presses the layers together until they become solid rock. This kind of rock often holds a fossil, such as a shell.

The third kind forms from heat and squeezing. Deep underground, rock can be pressed and heated. It does not melt, but it changes into a new kind of rock.

If any rock melts, it becomes magma again, and the cycle continues. The rock cycle has no beginning and no end.

versions.title: The Rock Cycle
versions.text:
A mountain may look like it will stay the same forever. But the rocks inside it are slowly changing all the time. These changes are so slow that they can take millions of years. Rocks change from one type to another in a loop that never ends. It is called the rock cycle. Scientists sort rocks into three main types: igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic.

Igneous rock forms from melted rock. Deep inside the Earth, it is hot enough to melt rock into magma. When magma bursts out of a volcano, it is called lava. As the lava cools, it hardens into igneous rock. Near Madinah, there are huge lava fields covered with black igneous rock.

Sedimentary rock forms from tiny pieces of older rock. Wind, rain, and ice slowly break rocks into bits such as sand and mud, which are called sediment. In the desert, hot days and cold nights can also make rocks crack. Water and wind then carry the sediment away. This moving of rock pieces is called erosion. In lakes and seas, the sediment settles and piles up in layers. Over time, the weight of the top layers presses the lower ones together until they become solid rock. Sedimentary rock often holds fossils, such as shells. The tall cliffs near Riyadh are made of rock layers that formed under an old sea.

Metamorphic rock forms when heat and pressure change a rock deep under the ground. The rock does not melt, but it turns into a new type of rock. For example, limestone can turn into marble.

If any rock melts, it becomes magma again, and the cycle goes on. The heat inside the Earth and the wind and rain on its surface keep it moving. The rock cycle has no beginning and no end.

versions.title: The Rock Cycle
versions.text:
A mountain may appear as though it will remain unchanged forever, but the rocks inside it are gradually and continually changing. These transformations are so slow that they can require millions of years, as rocks transform from one type to another in a continuous loop known as the rock cycle. Geologists classify rocks into three principal types: igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic.

Igneous rock forms from molten rock. Deep inside the Earth, temperatures are high enough to melt rock into magma. When magma erupts from a volcano, it is called lava, and as the lava cools, it solidifies into igneous rock. Near Madinah, enormous lava fields are covered with dark igneous rock called basalt.

Sedimentary rock forms from tiny fragments of older rock. Wind, rain, and ice gradually break rocks into particles such as sand and mud, which are called sediment, and in the desert, hot days and cold nights can also cause rocks to crack. Water and wind then transport the sediment elsewhere, a process called erosion. In lakes and seas, the sediment settles and accumulates in layers, and eventually the weight of the upper layers compresses the lower ones until they become solid rock. Sedimentary rock frequently contains fossils, such as shells. The towering cliffs near Riyadh consist of rock layers that formed beneath an ancient sea.

Metamorphic rock forms when intense heat and pressure alter a rock deep underground. The rock does not melt, but it transforms into a different type of rock, as when limestone becomes marble.

If any rock melts, it becomes magma again, and the cycle continues. The heat inside the Earth and the weather on its surface keep the cycle moving. The rock cycle has no beginning and no end.

versions.title: The Rock Cycle
versions.text:
A mountain may appear as though it will remain unchanged forever, but the rocks within it are gradually transforming, even though these changes typically require millions of years. Rocks change from one type to another in a loop known as the rock cycle. Geologists sort them into three principal categories according to how they originate: igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic.

Igneous rock comes from melted material. Deep inside the Earth, temperatures are high enough to melt rock into magma, which is called lava when it erupts from a volcano. When magma cools slowly underground, it produces rock with large, visible crystals, such as granite, while lava that cools rapidly at the surface produces rock with microscopic crystals, such as basalt. Near Madinah, extensive volcanic fields are blanketed with dark basalt from ancient eruptions.

Sedimentary rock forms from tiny fragments of older rock. Through weathering, wind, rain, and ice gradually break down rocks into particles such as sand and mud, which are called sediment. In desert environments, the big difference between hot days and cold nights can also make rocks crack. Water and wind then carry the sediment elsewhere, a process known as erosion. In lakes and seas, the sediment settles and accumulates in horizontal layers, and the heavy weight of the upper layers eventually presses and cements the lower ones into solid rock. Sedimentary rock often preserves fossils, and the tall cliffs of the Tuwaiq Mountains near Riyadh, for example, consist of limestone layers that formed beneath an ancient sea.

Metamorphic rock forms when intense heat and pressure alter an existing rock deep underground, usually where huge sections of the Earth's crust collide. The rock does not melt, but its minerals rearrange into a different kind of rock, as when limestone becomes marble or when shale, a sedimentary rock made from compacted mud, becomes slate.

If any rock melts, it becomes magma once again, and the cycle continues. Two sources of energy power this process. One is the Earth's internal heat, which melts and transforms rock below the surface, and the other is the energy of the sun, which drives the weather that breaks rock apart above it. The rock cycle therefore has no beginning and no conclusion.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to find gold and jewels in the ground
Why volcanoes are the most dangerous places
How rocks slowly change from one kind to another
How to build a strong house out of stone
questions.why: The article explains how rocks melt, break apart, press together, and change, over and over, in the rock cycle.

wrong.A: The article does not talk about gold or jewels.
wrong.B: Volcanoes are mentioned, but the article is about how rocks change.
wrong.D: The article does not talk about building houses.

questions.stem: What is melted rock under the ground called?
options: Magma
Lava
Wet sand
Soft mud
questions.why: The article says hot, melted rock under the ground is called magma.

wrong.B: Melted rock is called lava only after it comes out of the ground.
wrong.C: Sand is made of tiny broken bits of rock.
wrong.D: Mud is made of tiny bits that water carries away.

questions.stem: What can sometimes be found in rock that formed from layers?
options: Hot lava from a volcano
A fossil, such as a shell
Fresh water from a lake
Melted magma from deep down
questions.why: The article says rock made from layers may hold a fossil, like a shell.

wrong.A: Lava forms a different kind of rock when it cools.
wrong.C: The bits sink in lakes, but the rock does not hold fresh water.
wrong.D: Magma is melted rock deep underground, not something inside layered rock.

questions.stem: The article says sand and mud pile up in a layer. What is a layer?

A big fire inside the Earth
A strong wind in the desert
A flat sheet on top of another
questions.why: In the article, bits pile up into a layer, and more layers form on top, like flat sheets stacked up.

wrong.A: A layer is piled up, not dug out.
wrong.B: The heat inside the Earth is not a layer.
wrong.C: Wind breaks rocks, but it is not a layer.

questions.stem: What happens when lava cools?
options: It gets hard and becomes new rock.
It turns into sand and mud.
It melts into magma again.
It slowly becomes a fossil shell.
questions.why: The article says the lava cools, gets hard, and becomes new rock.

wrong.B: Sand and mud come from wind and rain breaking rock.
wrong.C: Cooling makes lava hard; melting is the opposite.
wrong.D: Fossils come from plants or animals, not cooled lava.

questions.stem: There are big fields of black rock near Madinah. What can you tell about that place?
options: It was once at the bottom of a lake.
Lava came out of the ground there long ago.
Wind and rain have never touched it.
It is the only place where rocks change.
questions.why: The article says the black rock near Madinah formed when lava cooled, so lava must have come out there long ago.

wrong.A: Rock from lake layers is made of sand and mud, not lava.
wrong.C: Wind and rain hit rocks everywhere.
wrong.D: The article says rocks change all over the Earth.

questions.stem: Noor finds a rock with a shell fossil in a dry desert. What can she infer?
options: Someone dropped a shell there last week.
The shell grew inside the rock.
Lava made the shell.
Water covered that place long ago.
questions.why: Rock with fossils forms from layers that pile up in lakes or seas, so water must have covered that place long ago.

wrong.A: A fossil is very old and is part of the rock.
wrong.B: Shells come from sea animals, not from rocks.
wrong.C: Lava is very hot rock and does not make shells.

questions.stem: Why does the author say the rock cycle has no start and no end?
options: To show that no one knows about rocks
To show that rocks keep changing over and over
To say that rocks never change at all
To explain how to draw a circle with no start or end
questions.why: Saying it has no start and no end shows that any rock can keep changing into another kind, again and again.

wrong.A: The article explains a lot that people know about rocks.
wrong.C: The article shows that rocks do change.
wrong.D: The article is about rocks, not drawing.

LOW.prompt: Choose one way that new rock forms. Tell how it happens, step by step, using details from the article.
checklist: I chose one way that rock forms.
I told the steps in the right order.
I used at least two details from the article.
LOW.modelAnswer: Igneous rock forms when magma erupts from a volcano as hot lava. As the lava cools, it slowly hardens into solid igneous rock. Near Madinah, there are huge fields covered with this kind of black rock, showing how this is part of the ongoing rock cycle.

keyWords.definition: formed when hot, melted rock cools and hardens
keyWords.example: The black igneous rock felt rough and heavy in my hand.

keyWords.definition: formed from layers of sand, mud, or shells pressed together over time
keyWords.example: You can see stripes in sedimentary rock where the layers formed.

keyWords.definition: formed when heat and pressure change one kind of rock into another

keyWords.definition: tiny pieces of rock, sand, or mud that are carried and dropped by water or wind
keyWords.example: After the flood, a thick layer of sediment covered the road.

keyWords.definition: the moving away of rock and soil by water, wind, or ice
keyWords.example: Planting trees can help stop erosion on a hillside.

wrong.C: Wind, rain, ice, heat, and pressure also change rocks.
wrong.D: The article mentions marble as an example, not as the main rock of Saudi Arabia.

Sedimentary

wrong.D: Pressing layers together makes sedimentary rock.

Lava flowing over them

wrong.D: Fossils do not turn into lava with age.

questions.stem: How does the author organize most of the article?

By listing problems and solutions
By giving each type of rock its own paragraph
By comparing rocks on Earth and the moon

wrong.D: The moon is not mentioned in the article.

MID.prompt: Imagine you are a grain of sand. Describe your journey through the rock cycle, using at least three key words from the article.
checklist: I described at least two stages of the rock cycle in order.
I used at least three key words correctly.
I included facts from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: I start as a tiny piece of sedimentary rock broken off a cliff by wind and rain, a process called erosion. The sediment that I become gets carried away and settles in layers at the bottom of a sea, where the weight above slowly presses me into solid sedimentary rock again. If heat and pressure later push down on me, I could change into a new metamorphic rock without ever melting.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how energy from inside the Earth and energy from the sun work together to keep the rock cycle going. Use evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained the role of each source of energy.
I supported my explanation with at least two examples from the article.
I used key words such as weathering, erosion, and pressure correctly.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Energy from inside the Earth keeps the rock cycle going by melting rock into magma, which later cools into igneous rock like the lava fields near Madinah, and by producing the heat and pressure that transform buried rock into metamorphic rock such as marble. Energy from the sun drives weathering and erosion at the surface, since hot days and cold nights crack rocks apart and wind and rain then carry the resulting sediment away to form layered sedimentary rock, like the cliffs near Riyadh. Together, these two energy sources make sure no rock stays the same forever, since any rock can eventually melt back into magma and begin the cycle again.
